Local projections and the LP versus VAR trade-off

Source: vignettes/local-projections.Rmd
local-projections.Rmd

1. Definition and derivation

1.1 From direct forecasts to impulse responses

Write the hh-step-ahead conditional expectation of yt+hy_{t+h} given the information at tt. A VAR obtains it by iterating the one-step model hh times. Jordà (2005) instead regresses yt+hy_{t+h}directly on the time-tt information, one regression per horizon h=0,1,…,Hh=0,1,\dots,H and response yky_k: yk,t+h=αh+βhst+γh′wt+et+h,h=0,1,…,H, y_{k,t+h}=\alpha_{h}+\beta_{h}\,s_t+\gamma_{h}'w_t+e_{t+h},\qquad h=0,1,\dots,H, where sts_t is the shock (or the variable being shocked), wtw_t collects controls (lags of the system, optionally contemporaneous variables) and βh\beta_h is the response at horizon hh to a unit change in sts_t: βh=∂E[yk,t+h∣st,wt]/∂st\beta_h=\partial\,E[y_{k,t+h}\mid s_t,w_t]/\partial s_t. Since wtw_t holds what must be held fixed for sts_t to be as good as randomly assigned, the coefficient is a causal response whenever sts_t is exogenous conditional on wtw_t, and nothing else about the dynamics is assumed. lp() runs the H+1H+1 regressions for all responses at once in C++ (cpp_lp).

1.2 Why the residuals are moving averages

Iterating the data-generating process forward, et+he_{t+h} contains every innovation that arrives between t+1t+1 and t+ht+h (the hh-step forecast error). In a correctly specified model it is therefore an MA(h−1h-1) process even when the innovations are i.i.d.: et+he_{t+h} and et+h−je_{t+h-j} share innovations for j<hj<h. Residuals are serially correlated by construction, the more so at long horizons, and ordinary OLS standard errors are wrong; heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust (HAC) errors are required. In practice the exact MA order is unknown (the model is misspecified for hh large), which is why the default truncation L=h+1L=h+1 is a deliberately generous upper bound.

1.3 Identification and the link to the Cholesky VAR

Identification enters through sts_t and wtw_t.

  • Recursive (Cholesky) scheme. Let sts_t be the policy rate and put in wtw_t the current values of the variables ordered before it (contemp) plus lags. Then βh\beta_h is the response to a shock with unit impact on the rate. Plagborg-Møller and Wolf (2021) show that, at the population level and with the same lags, this equals Θhej/Θ0jj\Theta_h e_j/\Theta_0^{jj}, the Cholesky impulse response of a VAR normalised to a unit impact on variable jj, which in varm is irf(normalise = normalise_to("rate", "rate", size = 1)). Variables ordered after the shock are left out of contemp. The recursive LP and the Cholesky VAR therefore estimate the same object; they differ only in how they use the data (section 6).
  • Unit-impact normalisation. When shock is a column of Y, the regressor is the variable itself, so β0=1\beta_0=1 for that variable by construction and the response is per one unit of the variable, not per standard deviation. To convert, multiply by the standard deviation of the structural shock.
  • Observed or external shock. If shock is a numeric vector of length TT (a narrative or high-frequency shock series), it enters as sts_t with its own lags in wtw_t; βh\beta_h is the response per unit of that series.
  • External instrument (LP-IV). If sts_t is endogenous, instrument it by ztz_t (iv =): two-stage least squares at each horizon, with β0\beta_0 normalised to one (Stock and Watson, 2018; Ramey, 2016). The controls wtw_t serve as exogenous regressors in both stages.

1.4 Inference as implemented

Let xtx_{t} be the regressors of horizon hh (mm columns, n=T−p−hn=T-p-h observations), êt+h\hat e_{t+h} the residuals and qt=xt′(X′X)−1e1q_t=x_t'(X'X)^{-1}e_1 the influence weight of β̂h\hat\beta_h (in 2SLS the fitted values replace xtx_t). With gt=qtêt+hg_t=q_t\hat e_{t+h}: Var̂(β̂h)=c[∑tgt2+2∑l=1L(1−lL+1)∑t>lgtgt−l]. \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\beta_h)=c\Big[\sum_t g_t^2+2\sum_{l=1}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{l}{L+1}\Big)\sum_{t>l}g_tg_{t-l}\Big].

  • se = "nw": Newey-West with Bartlett weights 1−l/(L+1)1-l/(L+1) and truncation L=h+1L=h+1 by default (nw_lag changes it, e.g. to a fixed value across horizons), c=1c=1, or c=n/(n−m)c=n/(n-m) with dof_adjust = TRUE.
  • se = "hc": Eicker-Huber-White HC1, i.e. L=0L=0 and c=n/(n−m)c=n/(n-m) always; nw_lag is ignored. It treats the residuals as serially uncorrelated and is not valid by itself at h>0h>0 unless lags are augmented.
  • lag_augment = TRUE: Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2021) show that if one extra lag is added to the controls and not interpreted, the heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are valid without HAC, uniformly over stationary and persistent data, and over horizons. The reason is that the extra lag makes the regressor of interest asymptotically orthogonal to the serial correlation of the residual. The option adds one lag to lags and switches se to "hc"; lags and nw_lag then no longer mean what they did, so fit$lags reports the lag count actually used.

1.5 Cumulative responses

For a variable in differences, the response of the level at horizon hh is the cumulative sum, estimated directly by regressing ∑j=0hΔyt+j\sum_{j=0}^{h}\Delta y_{t+j} on sts_t and controls (cumulative =). This is also more efficient than summing the estimated βj\beta_j and has a direct standard error. Section 5 gives an example.

2. LP on yraw versus the VAR

We estimate the response to a policy-rate shock under the recursive ordering inflation, unemployment, rate, with two lags, both ways:

Variables are named with tidyselect syntax (bare names, strings or c()/all_of()). glance() summarises the specification and tidy() returns one row per horizon, response and band level:

l <- lp(yraw, shock = rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp))
l
#> <lpm> local projection of infl, unemp, rate on 'rate', horizons 0..16 (2 lags, NW)
#>       infl   unemp    rate
#> 0   0.0000  0.0000  1.0000
#> 1  -0.0589 -0.0295  0.7650
#> 4  -0.0217  0.0284  0.5960
#> 8  -0.0745  0.1937  0.1735
#> 12 -0.4550  0.1486 -0.1578
#> 16 -0.5689  0.0709 -0.4345
glance(l)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   shock horizon  lags se_type iv     nobs
#>   <chr>   <int> <int> <chr>   <lgl> <dbl>
#> 1 rate       16     2 nw      FALSE   213
head(tidy(l), 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 7
#>   horizon response  estimate std.error level  conf.low conf.high
#>     <int> <fct>        <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1       0 infl     -1.24e-14  1.37e-13   0.9 -2.39e-13  2.14e-13
#> 2       1 infl     -5.89e- 2  4.20e- 2   0.9 -1.28e- 1  1.01e- 2
#> 3       2 infl     -6.16e- 2  7.23e- 2   0.9 -1.81e- 1  5.74e- 2
#> 4       3 infl     -3.15e- 2  1.05e- 1   0.9 -2.04e- 1  1.41e- 1
fit <- varm(yraw, p = 2)
v <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 300,
         normalise = normalise_to("rate", "rate", size = 1))

At h=0h=0 the response of the shock variable is one and that of every variable in contemp is zero, by construction (they are regressors); their reported standard errors are numerical zeros of order 10−1410^{-14}, not real precision, so ignore the width of the band there.

autoplot() returns a ggplot that takes ordinary ggplot2 layers. To overlay the VAR we bind the two tidy tibbles:

var90 <- subset(tidy(v), shock == "rate" & level == 0.9)
autoplot(l) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), data = var90, fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = var90, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "LP (blue, 90% HAC) versus VAR (grey, 90% bootstrap)")

The LP point estimates track the VAR responses at short horizons and become jagged at long horizons, with much wider bands: the signature of the bias-variance trade-off analysed in section 6. Because each horizon is a separate regression, nothing forces the LP response to be smooth.

Speed is rarely a concern: on an Apple M4 Pro a full three-response lp() with H=16H=16 takes about 0.5 ms per call, against about 0.05 ms for the OLS varm() (mean over repeated calls; your machine will differ).

Economic intuition / how to use it

The LP is a direct regression: “if the rate is 1 point higher today, by how much does unemployment differ hh quarters later, controlling for the past and for current inflation and unemployment?”. It gives the sign and rough size of the effect with minimal assumptions about the dynamics, a good diagnostic alongside the VAR. A large disagreement between LP and VAR at medium horizons is informative: it flags a VAR lag order that is too short (misspecification) or an LP with too little data.

3. Standard errors: HAC versus heteroskedasticity-robust 

se_nw <- lp(yraw, rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), se = "nw")
se_dof <- lp(yraw, rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), se = "nw", dof_adjust = TRUE)
se_hc <- lp(yraw, rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), se = "hc")
se_la <- lp(yraw, rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), lag_augment = TRUE)
round(rbind(`Newey-West (h+1)` = se_nw$se[c(2, 5, 9, 13, 17), "unemp"],
            `NW + dof_adjust`  = se_dof$se[c(2, 5, 9, 13, 17), "unemp"],
            `HC1`              = se_hc$se[c(2, 5, 9, 13, 17), "unemp"],
            `lag-augmented HC` = se_la$se[c(2, 5, 9, 13, 17), "unemp"]), 3)
#>                      1     4     8    12    16
#> Newey-West (h+1) 0.045 0.081 0.066 0.101 0.118
#> NW + dof_adjust  0.046 0.083 0.067 0.103 0.121
#> HC1              0.044 0.089 0.101 0.128 0.108
#> lag-augmented HC 0.046 0.093 0.105 0.130 0.109

(Columns are horizons 1, 4, 8, 12, 16.) The three estimators differ most at medium horizons: here Newey-West is smaller than the heteroskedasticity-robust HC1 at horizons 4 to 12. Newey-West with a bandwidth that is a large share of TT is known to be biased downward and to produce size distortions in small samples (use dof_adjust = TRUE for an n/(n−m)n/(n-m) factor), and HC1 alone ignores the MA(hh) error structure, so neither is dependable by itself at long horizons. The lag-augmented HC standard errors have a theoretical justification that does not depend on persistence or on a bandwidth: the extra lag is a control only and its coefficient is not reported. They are a sensible default when the data may be persistent or the horizon is a sizeable fraction of the sample, but as the simulation below shows they do not remove the finite-sample shortfall.

When does lag augmentation help? A small Monte Carlo

Lag augmentation matters when the data are persistent. We simulate a bivariate VAR(1) with a near-unit root, T=200T=200, a recursive identification, and compute the coverage of the pointwise 90% band for the response of yy to a unit impulse in xx, for Newey-West and for lag-augmented HC errors. (300 replications: coverage figures carry a Monte Carlo error of about ±0.02\pm 0.02.)

set.seed(11)
A <- matrix(c(0.97, 0.15, 0, 0.6), 2, 2, byrow = FALSE)   # persistent x, y driven by x
Pm <- t(chol(matrix(c(1, 0.3, 0.3, 1), 2)))
hz <- c(1, 4, 8, 12)
truth_aug <- sapply(0:12, function(h) { M <- diag(2); for (i in seq_len(h)) M <- A %*% M; (M %*% Pm[, 1] / Pm[1, 1])[2] })[hz + 1]
cover <- function(la, R = 300) {
  hit <- matrix(0, R, length(hz))
  for (r in seq_len(R)) {
    e <- matrix(rnorm(2 * 300), 300) %*% t(Pm); Yb <- matrix(0, 300, 2)
    for (t in 2:300) Yb[t, ] <- A %*% Yb[t - 1, ] + e[t, ]
    Yb <- Yb[101:300, ]; colnames(Yb) <- c("x", "y")
    f <- lp(Yb, x, horizon = 12, lags = 1, responses = y, lag_augment = la, level = 0.9)
    hit[r, ] <- truth_aug >= f$bands[hz + 1, 1, 1] & truth_aug <= f$bands[hz + 1, 1, 2]
  }
  colMeans(hit)
}
round(rbind(`Newey-West` = cover(FALSE), `lag-augmented HC` = cover(TRUE)) |> `colnames<-`(paste0("h=", hz)), 2)
#>                   h=1  h=4  h=8 h=12
#> Newey-West       0.91 0.85 0.82 0.81
#> lag-augmented HC 0.88 0.88 0.82 0.80

Coverage is at or below the 0.90 target at every horizon beyond the first (roughly 0.80 to 0.88), and in this design lag augmentation does not clearly improve on Newey-West at long horizons: the differences of 0.01 to 0.03 are within Monte Carlo error, and at h=1h=1 Newey-West is actually closer to nominal. What lag augmentation buys is mainly theoretical, namely validity that does not depend on persistence or on a bandwidth choice. In the whole-path (sup-t) simulation of vignette("lp-advanced") it helps somewhat (0.84 against 0.78 at a nominal 0.90) but does not close the gap. It is no cure for a short sample with a highly persistent regressor, where the effective sample is small, and it costs a slightly larger standard error because the extra lag is estimated and not used. Treat all LP bands at long horizons as somewhat optimistic.

4. External shocks and LP-IV

When sts_t is an externally identified shock series (narrative, high-frequency, or a VAR residual from another study), pass it as shock. When the regressor is the policy rate itself but the shock is only observed through an instrument ztz_t, pass iv. We illustrate with a constructed instrument: the estimated Cholesky policy shock plus independent noise, mimicking a noisy high-frequency measure (this is a simulation device; yraw contains no instrument).

u <- resid(fit)[, 3]                             # "true" shock from the VAR
z <- c(rep(0, 2), u) + rnorm(nrow(y), sd = sd(u))   # noisy measure of the shock
l_ols <- lp(yraw, rate, horizon = 8, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp))
l_iv  <- lp(yraw, rate, horizon = 8, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp), iv = cbind(z = z))
l_ext <- lp(y, shock = z, horizon = 8, lags = 2)  # z as the shock itself (units of z, no normalisation)
round(rbind(`OLS, recursive` = l_ols$estimate[, "unemp"],
            `IV (z)`         = l_iv$estimate[, "unemp"],
            `external shock` = l_ext$estimate[, "unemp"]), 3)
#>                     0      1      2      3      4      5      6     7     8
#> OLS, recursive  0.000 -0.030 -0.079 -0.029  0.028  0.051  0.086 0.149 0.194
#> IV (z)          0.000  0.015 -0.047 -0.009 -0.004  0.008  0.070 0.134 0.182
#> external shock -0.086 -0.107 -0.141 -0.113 -0.080 -0.054 -0.003 0.033 0.076

The IV and OLS results differ because the IV does not require the recursive timing assumption (only that ztz_t is correlated with the policy shock and orthogonal to other shocks). The external-shock row is a reduced-form response per unit of zz; to compare it with the others divide by its impact response on the rate (l_ext$estimate[1, "rate"]). lp() does not report instrument strength: check the first-stage FF statistic yourself before trusting LP-IV (a weak instrument makes the IV estimates and their normal bands unreliable at every horizon).

5. Cumulative responses

For a variable in differences, cumulate the left-hand side. Below, inflation enters in differences and we recover the response of its level:

yd <- cbind(dinfl = diff(y[, "infl"]), y[-1, c("unemp", "rate")])
lc <- lp(yd, rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(dinfl, unemp), cumulative = dinfl)
l_lev <- lp(yraw, rate, horizon = 16, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp))   # inflation in levels
cum <- rbind(cbind(method = "cumulated LP of dinfl", subset(tidy(lc), response == "dinfl" & level == 0.9)),
             cbind(method = "LP of inflation level", subset(tidy(l_lev), response == "infl" & level == 0.9)))
ggplot(cum, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = method, fill = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(2), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(2), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to a rate shock",
       title = "Response of the level of inflation") +
  theme_varm()

6. LP versus VAR: the bias-variance trade-off

Population equivalence. With enough lags both estimate the same IRF. Plagborg-Møller and Wolf (2021) show that LP and VAR(∞\infty) responses coincide; the difference is statistical. A VAR with pp lags imposes that the response at horizon hh is ei′ΦhPeje_i'\Phi_hPe_j, a nonlinear function of the first pp matrices (parsimony, smoothness, extrapolation of short-run dynamics to long horizons). An LP imposes nothing. Hence:

VAR(pp) LP
bias grows with horizon if pp is too small (misspecification) small at all horizons
variance low (parameters pooled across horizons) high at long horizons (one regression per horizon, overlapping MA(hh) errors)
shape smooth, monotone decay erratic
efficiency under correct model efficient inefficient
extension closed-form FEVD, HD, forecasts nonlinear/state-dependent versions are straightforward

Li, Plagborg-Møller and Wolf (2024) confirm in thousands of DGPs that this trade-off is systematic: LP has lower bias but much higher variance, and the mean-squared-error ranking depends on the persistence of the data, the sample size and the horizon. We reproduce the logic in a small Monte Carlo. The DGP is the VAR(2) fitted to yraw (so it has the persistence of real macro data), with T=200T=200 and a recursive identification. We estimate the response of unemployment to a unit policy-rate shock by (a) the correctly specified VAR(2), (b) a misspecified VAR(1) and (c) LP with two lags.

true_fit <- fit; P <- t(chol(true_fit$Sigma))
sim <- function(Tn, burn = 100, p = 2) {
  n <- Tn + burn; Y <- matrix(0, n, 3)
  for (t in (p + 1):n) Y[t, ] <- c(Y[t - 1, ], Y[t - 2, ], 1) %*% true_fit$B + drop(P %*% rnorm(3))
  colnames(Y) <- colnames(y); Y[-seq_len(burn), ]
}
nm <- normalise_to("rate", "rate", size = 1)
H <- 24; hs <- c(4, 8, 16, 24)
truth <- irf(true_fit, horizon = H, ci = "none", normalise = nm)$estimate["unemp", "rate", hs + 1]
R <- 500
est <- array(NA_real_, c(R, 3, length(hs)), dimnames = list(NULL, c("VAR(2)", "VAR(1)", "LP(2)"), paste0("h=", hs)))
for (r in seq_len(R)) {
  Y <- sim(200)
  est[r, 1, ] <- irf(varm(Y, 2), horizon = H, ci = "none", normalise = nm)$estimate["unemp", "rate", hs + 1]
  est[r, 2, ] <- irf(varm(Y, 1), horizon = H, ci = "none", normalise = nm)$estimate["unemp", "rate", hs + 1]
  est[r, 3, ] <- lp(Y, rate, horizon = H, lags = 2, contemp = c(infl, unemp))$estimate[hs + 1, "unemp"]
}
bias <- apply(est, c(2, 3), mean) - rep(truth, each = 3)
sdv  <- apply(est, c(2, 3), sd)
rmse <- sqrt(bias^2 + sdv^2)
rbind(truth = round(truth, 3))
#>           4     8    16    24
#> truth 0.058 0.103 0.045 0.001
list(bias = round(bias, 3), sd = round(sdv, 3), rmse = round(rmse, 3))
#> $bias
#>           h=4    h=8   h=16   h=24
#> VAR(2)  0.014  0.001 -0.021 -0.017
#> VAR(1) -0.024 -0.070 -0.054 -0.043
#> LP(2)   0.000 -0.013 -0.016 -0.011
#> 
#> $sd
#>          h=4   h=8  h=16  h=24
#> VAR(2) 0.059 0.061 0.054 0.056
#> VAR(1) 0.048 0.057 0.064 0.073
#> LP(2)  0.083 0.096 0.115 0.131
#> 
#> $rmse
#>          h=4   h=8  h=16  h=24
#> VAR(2) 0.061 0.062 0.058 0.058
#> VAR(1) 0.053 0.091 0.083 0.085
#> LP(2)  0.083 0.097 0.116 0.132
stat <- list(`|bias|` = abs(bias), sd = sdv, rmse = rmse)
mc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(stat), function(w) {
  m <- stat[[w]]
  tibble::tibble(statistic = factor(w, names(stat)), method = rep(rownames(m), ncol(m)),
                 horizon = rep(hs, each = nrow(m)), value = as.vector(m))
}))
mc
#> # A tibble: 36 × 4
#>    statistic method horizon    value
#>    <fct>     <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 |bias|    VAR(2)       4 0.0141  
#>  2 |bias|    VAR(1)       4 0.0239  
#>  3 |bias|    LP(2)        4 0.000177
#>  4 |bias|    VAR(2)       8 0.00117 
#>  5 |bias|    VAR(1)       8 0.0704  
#>  6 |bias|    LP(2)        8 0.0130  
#>  7 |bias|    VAR(2)      16 0.0211  
#>  8 |bias|    VAR(1)      16 0.0536  
#>  9 |bias|    LP(2)       16 0.0161  
#> 10 |bias|    VAR(2)      24 0.0171  
#> # ℹ 26 more rows
ggplot(mc, aes(horizon, value, colour = method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~statistic) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(3), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = NULL) +
  theme_varm()

The results are what theory predicts: LP has small bias but a standard deviation 1.4 to 2.3 times larger (growing with the horizon), and the VAR(1) has a bias that is largest at medium horizons (its dynamics are too simple). The correctly specified VAR(2) has an RMSE of about 0.06 at every horizon, whereas the LP’s RMSE rises from 0.08 to 0.13. The misspecified VAR(1) is even slightly better than VAR(2) at h = 4, which is why parsimonious VARs often win in forecasting exercises.

compare_lp_var()

compare_lp_var() runs the comparison for you with the same lags and the same recursive ordering (column order of Y), normalising the VAR to a unit impact on the shock variable, and reports the difference in units of the LP standard error. With the default se, the printed summary is the mean $|{\rm LP}-{\rm VAR}|/\widehat{\rm se}_{\rm LP}$ over three horizon blocks; large values at long horizons point to VAR misspecification or to LP noise.

cmp <- compare_lp_var(yraw, shock = unemp, horizon = 12, lags = 2)
cmp
#> <lp_var_cmp> shock 'unemp', 2 lags; mean |LP - VAR| / se_LP by horizon block:
#>         infl  rate unemp
#> short  0.274 0.276 0.701
#> medium 0.498 0.152 0.344
#> long   0.189 0.519 0.500
cmp |>
  subset(response == "infl" & horizon %in% c(0, 4, 8, 12), select = c(horizon, lp, lp_se, var, diff, z)) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  round(3)
#>   horizon     lp lp_se    var   diff      z
#> 1       0  0.000 0.000  0.000  0.000 -0.329
#> 2       4 -0.904 0.240 -0.790 -0.114 -0.476
#> 3       8 -1.005 0.357 -0.815 -0.190 -0.533
#> 4      12 -0.675 0.318 -0.613 -0.062 -0.194

The result is a tibble with columns horizon, response, lp, lp_se, var, diff and z, so it goes straight into ggplot2:

ggplot(cmp, aes(horizon)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lp - 1.645 * lp_se, ymax = lp + 1.645 * lp_se), fill = varm_palette(1), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = lp, colour = "LP")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = var, colour = "VAR"), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~response, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(2), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to a unemployment shock") +
  theme_varm()

The h=0h=0 row is exact by construction (the response of a variable that is itself a regressor), with a numerical-zero standard error, so its z is not informative. Note that the shock here is unemployment (ordered second), so the only contemporaneous control is inflation. Two further points. First, the population equivalence is an asymptotic statement: with T≈250T\approx 250 the differences above are estimation noise, not a failure of the theory. Second, compare_lp_var() returns VAR point estimates; for a VAR band use irf(ci = "bootstrap") as in section 2.

Cross-checking against lpirfs

The recursive LP in lp() was compared with lpirfs::lp_lin(). The two agree closely, but they are not reconciled exactly: differences of up to about 0.03 appear at long horizons. We attribute them to sample alignment and the construction of the contemporaneous controls, but we have not confirmed this. If you need numbers that match lpirfs to the digit, use lpirfs; the discrepancy is small relative to the sampling error of an LP at those horizons (section 6, bands). The state-dependent version, by contrast, reproduces lpirfs::lp_nl to about 10−1210^{-12} under its timing = "lagged" convention (vignette("lp-advanced")).

When to prefer which

  • Prefer a VAR when the horizon is short or moderate, the sample is short, you want smooth responses with tight bands, FEVD/HD or forecasts, or the system is large (with shrinkage: vignette("bayesian-var")).
  • Prefer LP when robustness to misspecification matters more than precision: long horizons with a doubtful lag order, nonlinear or state-dependent effects (interaction terms are a regression away), an instrument for one shock in a big system (LP-IV needs no model of the other variables), or as a check on a VAR.
  • Use both. If they agree, report the VAR (more efficient); if they disagree at medium horizons, increase pp, or report the LP band as the honest one. A rule of thumb from the Monte Carlo literature: bias is the main concern at long horizons and small pp, variance at small TT and large KK.

7. Where to go next

  • vignette("lp-advanced"): state-dependent, smooth, panel and joint-inference (sup-t) LP, and direct forecasts.
  • vignette("choosing-a-method"): decision tables across the whole package.
  • vignette("identification"): Cholesky, long-run, sign and proxy identification for the VAR counterpart.
